Beyond Fuzzy Matching: Constraint-Guided Patch Presence Testing for Obfuscated Java Binaries

Patch presence testing (PPT) is critical for mitigating vulnerabilities introduced by the use of third-party libraries (TPLs) in Java programs. However, the widespread use of obfuscation significantly undermines its accuracy by altering patch-relevant features. To preserve feature consistency before and after obfuscation for reliable comparison, existing studies summarize patch digests using several representative \textit{fuzzy features}. These fuzzy features, designed to generalize obfuscation-prone details, have proven effective in TPL detection. Nevertheless, this approach faces limitations when directly applied to PPT, where finer features are needed to capture subtle patch changes. Although patch digests facilitate feature matching under obfuscation-induced code changes with high efficiency, methods with similar semantic structures—common in TPLs due to factors such as overriding and inheritance—often exhibit identical digests. Relying solely on feature similarity without considering method constraints often results in inaccurate outcomes.

To tackle the aforementioned challenges, this paper presents \textit{PScan}, a constraint-guided patch presence testing tool capable of detecting patches in both standard and obfuscated Java binaries (i.e., executables of Java programs). PScan first defines a set of actual constraints that must be satisfied during Java method matching. Guided by these constraints, it maps methods containing critical patch information to their obfuscated counterparts and then leverages these mappings to refine the associated fuzzy features into concrete expressions. Furthermore, leveraging the formalized constraints, PScan formulates the patch digest matching process as a binary integer programming (BIP) model to precisely identify correct method matches. Extensive evaluations on public datasets show that PScan outperforms state-of-the-art methods, improving accuracy by at least 15.0 percentage points and achieving an overall accuracy of 97.1%. Our experiments also reveal that, with these constraints, PScan reduces the method mismatch rate to 1.5%, a 16.9 percentage point reduction relative to the baseline.
